name: Git Internals & Versioning Workflows
tagline: A content-addressable filesystem wrapped in an immutable DAG of snapshots, where branches are 41-byte pointers and trunk-based workflows keep CI/CD fast.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of Git—from SHA-1/SHA-256 blobs, trees, and commits to packfiles, partial clones, and trunk-based release hygiene.

spark.summary: Git is a content-addressable filesystem wrapped in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of immutable snapshots, where branches are 41-byte pointers and continuous delivery relies on keeping that DAG shallow, trunk-aligned, and decoupled from feature release via runtime flags.
spark.keyTakeaway: Every commit hashes its root tree, parent pointers, and metadata into an immutable SHA-1/SHA-256 node; mastering object storage, packfile deltas, and short-lived trunk branches eliminates merge hell and keeps CI/CD lead times under an hour.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Git is not a diff tracker—it is a **content-addressable object store** (`.git/objects`) wrapped in a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Git DAG: Commit -> Root Tree -> Subtrees & Blobs (Commit (SHA-1/256) -> Root Tree -> Subtree (src/) -> Blob); Short-Lived PR -> Merge Queue Speculative CI -> Immutable Tag (PR (<24h Branch) -> MERGE QUEUE -> MAIN (Green)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Every team must choose how PRs land on `main`—and whether to organize services in a monorepo or polyrepo. High-velocity engineering orgs enforce **pre-receive hooks** (rejecting blobs `>10 MB` and secrets), route PRs through a **Merge Queue** that tests the post-merge state before.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how Git workflows connect to feature flags, canary rollouts, and immutable infrastructure.

learningJourney.title: What is Git's Content-Addressable Object Model
learningJourney.explanation:
Git is not a diff tracker—it is a **content-addressable object store** (`.git/objects`) wrapped in a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)**. Every file (`blob`), directory (`tree`), snapshot (`commit`), and signed `tag` is zlib-compressed and keyed by the SHA-1 (40 hex chars) or SHA-256 hash of `'<type> <size>\0<content>'`.

Git reconciles three trees: the **Working Tree** (disk files), the **Index/Staging Area** (`.git/index` binary cache with `stat()` mtime/inode metadata), and **HEAD** (a symbolic ref pointing to the active 41-byte branch file under `.git/refs/heads/`).

sectionDiagram.title: Git DAG: Commit -> Root Tree -> Subtrees & Blobs

cards.label: Deduplication
cards.detail: Unchanged files across 1,000 commits share the exact same blob SHA-1 hash.

cards.label: 41-Byte Branches
cards.detail: Creating a branch writes a single 40-char commit hash + newline in .git/refs/heads/.

cards.label: Packfile Deltas
cards.detail: git gc packs loose objects into delta-compressed .pack + .idx files for fast transport.

sectionDiagram.summary: Every commit points to a complete root tree; unchanged subtrees and blobs are reused by hash with zero duplication.

learningJourney.title: Why Understanding Internals Solves Monorepo & Merge Bottlenecks
learningJourney.explanation: Treating Git as a black box leads to 48 GB `.git` histories bloated by accidental binaries, 14-minute CI clones, and tangled long-lived branches. Knowing how `packfiles`, `reflog`, and `--filter=blob:none` partial clones work turns slow monorepos and broken rebases into deterministic sub-minute operations.

learningJourney.title: Where Git Excels (and Where Git LFS / Object Storage Belongs)
learningJourney.explanation: Git's packfile delta compression is built for text source code and IaC; large incompressible binaries destroy packfile performance.

benefits: Cryptographic provenance from commit SHA to CI/CD artifact with <24h short-lived branches.
costs: Requires runtime feature flags to merge incomplete work safely to `main`.

benefits: Use Git LFS or S3/artifact registries so `.git` packfiles stay lean.
costs: A single 500 MB binary committed to history permanently bloats every developer's clone unless rewritten with `git filter-repo`.

benefits: Time-series stores or Iceberg lakehouses handle append-only machine logs natively.
costs: Creating thousands of automated commits/hour degrades packfile delta chains and `git status`.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Monorepo Partial Clones, Safe Force-Push & Reflog Recovery
learningJourney.explanation: Keep monorepo CI fast with blobless clones + cone-mode sparse checkout, protect shared branches with `--force-with-lease` (never raw `--force`), and recover dropped commits via `git reflog` before the 90-day GC window expires.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```bash
# Fast CI checkout on a 48 GB monorepo (downloads commits/trees only, fetches needed blobs)
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/org/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout set --cone services/checkout packages/shared-proto

# Safe rebase push: aborts if a teammate pushed new commits to the remote branch
git push --force-with-lease origin feat/checkout-v2

# Automated binary search to pinpoint the exact commit causing a latency regression
git bisect start HEAD v2.14.0
git bisect run ./scripts/bench-regression.sh
```
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Merge vs. Rebase vs. Squash-and-Merge
learningJourney.explanation: Every team must choose how PRs land on `main`—and whether to organize services in a monorepo or polyrepo.

benefits: One atomic, revertible commit per PR; keeps `main` linear and `git bisect` clean.
costs: Collapses granular WIP commit boundaries inside large multi-author PRs.

benefits: Linear history with zero merge-commit noise while preserving individual atomic commits.
costs: Rewrites commit SHAs; unsafe on shared branches without `--force-with-lease`.

benefits: Atomic cross-service refactors and unified proto/API contracts.
costs: Needs partial clones, sparse checkout, and a merge queue (e.g., GitHub Merge Queue) to prevent broken `main`.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production CI/CD: Pre-Receive Hooks + Merge Queue + Trunk Flags
learningJourney.explanation: High-velocity engineering orgs enforce **pre-receive hooks** (rejecting blobs `>10 MB` and secrets), route PRs through a **Merge Queue** that tests the post-merge state before advancing `main`, and keep branches `<24h` via **feature flags**.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should engineers always use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `git push --force` after rebasing a branch?

options.text: `--force-with-lease` aborts the push if the remote branch has new commits you haven't fetched yet, preventing you from overwriting a teammate's work
options.feedback: Correct: it checks that the remote ref matches your expected SHA before updating.

options.text: `--force-with-lease` automatically merges conflicting commits without rebasing
options.feedback: It does not merge; it safely rejects the force push if the remote moved.
It is a safety check on remote refs, not a compression option.
